author: ohtadmin
title: Native islander conducting in Midwest
text:
A music prodigy native to Jamestown, known for playing in front of dozens at St. Matthew’s, is now helping to conduct the second-oldest professional symphony orchestra in the United States.
Sam Hollister, who was named the assistant conductor of the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra in September 2024, also is the music director of the Fred M. Haigh Youth Orchestra. While Hollister says he misses the ocean, he has enjoyed the “energy, commitment and passion” of the Midwest.
“There’s something very special about the people here and the way they invest in this orchestra,” he said. “Everyone knows the symphony. Everyone is very invested in it.”
Hollister said he was hired following a “serendipitous chain of events” while he was working on his doctoral degree at the Yale School of Music. Conductor Leonard Slatkin, who had previously been the director of the St. Louis Symphony, was invited as a guest to conduct the Yale Philharmonia. He asked Hollister to conduct dress rehearsals.
Pleased with what he saw, Hollister was invited during the 2023-24 winter to St. Louis, where Slatkin still served as a guest conductor. At the time, there was a vacancy in the assistant position, and a guest was filling the role every week.
Hollister conducted the dress rehearsals for a week. In the spring, he was invited back as a guest.
That is when Hollister’s guest role ended. He was hired as the full-time assistant in the fall.
Hollister studies every piece of music that the conductor plays, even if he is not scheduled to conduct, so he can fill in if something should come up, like a delayed flight. The orchestra performs multiple concerts each week, spanning a variety of genres, from classical to film score to pop music.
Additionally, Hollister has some other roles with the orchestra. He is a consultant for the orchestra and listens to the symphony from every corner of the auditorium, takes notes about balance, and gives feedback during rehearsals. He also conducts the symphony orchestra at special performances such as educational gigs, family concerts and tour engagements.
Lastly, Hollister supports other departments such as marketing and philanthropy, and hosts a podcast for the symphony called “Noted.”
Hollister said he conducts the orchestra on stage every week. He will conduct the orchestra during film screenings where the orchestra will perform a score of a film while it is projected behind them. He also conducts the orchestra to accompany guest artists, such as the Norwegian soprano Sissel Kyrkjebo, known for her work on the film “Titanic.” Hollister said conducting a symphonic orchestra is a “remarkably difficult experience to describe.”
“It’s a stressful and focused experience,” Hollister said.
The Fred M. Haigh Youth Orchestra is one of the four ensembles that are part of the Symphony Orchestra, the others being the symphony and two choruses. As director for the youth orchestra, he conducts three concerts annually for the ensemble featuring musicians ages 12-22.
“The repertoire this youth orchestra plays, the level is so extraordinary, I feel so fortunate that I get to work with this group,” Hollister said. “They’re very inspiring. We get to program extraordinary music.”
For their latest show, Hollister said the youth orchestra was rehearsing the entire seven-movement suite of Gustav Holst’s “The Planets.”
Hollister chooses the repertoire that the youth orchestra performs at these concerts, which includes classic symphonies by Brahms and Tchaikovsky and the work of contemporary composers like Unsuk Chin. Hollister said his thought process for selection centers on three ideas, the first being that he chooses music that inspires the musicians in “a vivid way.”
“We’re at a threshold moment in their lives, where many of them will go on to study music, but some of them won’t,” he said. “It needs to be music that inspires and serves them as they go onto whatever the next chapter of their lives may be.”
His second tenet is that the music chosen must involve everyone in the orchestra, from the full percussion to low brass. The last is that the music needs to be a challenge for the musicians’ skill sets while pushing the envelope enough that the musicians wouldn’t wind up disappointed with their work.
“It needs to push them, but just the right amount to help them grow and not feel let down in the end,” he said,
Hollister said the youth orchestra has been his favorite part of working with the orchestra since he joined. He said the youth orchestra plays at a “remarkably high” level, and he and his predecessors as music director have programmed challenging repertoire for the young musicians.
“It’s an endless source of inspiration that we come together for our first rehearsal, and they come very prepared,” Hollister said. “The expression and interpretation that we can then explore over ten rehearsals is unbelievably rewarding and fun. If I’m ever feeling a little on the edge of burnt out or overwhelmed, I always feel reenergized and recharged after a rehearsal with the youth orchestra.”
Hollister had a prolific music career even before he graduated from North Kingstown High School as the valedictorian of the class of 2014. He started playing piano at age 4, and became a student of University of Rhode Island music professor Manabu Takasawa four years later.
As a teenager, Hollister regularly performed with Takasawa’s college students at collaborative concerts held by URI and the Jamestown Community Piano Association. He also performed at URI’s annual Piano Extravaganza, and as part of the pit orchestra during high school musical productions.
Hollister said his piano studies with Takasawa were “the most formative element” of his upbringing as a musician. He noted that because of his work with the Aurora Collective, he learned administrative, programming and fundraising skills that he has carried over to his work with the symphony. He said the Jamestown community was “warm and familial” towards music and his artistic endeavors before he left for college and his new job.
“That was a rare gift, I think, to be growing up in a town where, as I described here with our symphony orchestra, everyone is so committed and invested. It feels the same is true with Jamestowners and our community organizations.”
Following high school, Hollister attended Yale University, where he graduated with his bachelor’s degree in 2018. He earned his master’s degree in orchestral conducting and musical pedagogy from the Peabody Conservatory of Music at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, and is currently working on his doctorate in musical arts from Yale.
Back home in Jamestown, Hollister formed a music nonprofit, the Aurora Collective in 2018, and was part of two concerts in town in early 2020, weeks before the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown.
Hollister is still in the midst of completing his doctoral degree at Yale, and will eventually defend a dossier of professional work before he earns his degree.
Next year, Hollister will conduct several St. Louis concerts, including “Music Without Boundaries” in March, which will feature soloists for instruments that are not ordinarily featured in an orchestra, such as the accordion.
